did_you_know.text: Did you know? Micah introduces his prophecy as “the word of the LORD,” spoken during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.
Did you know? At the beginning of the prophecy, Micah calls on all peoples and the whole earth to listen, presenting the LORD as a witness from His holy temple.
Did you know? The LORD’s appearance is described vividly: He comes out of His place, descends, and treads upon the heights of the earth.
Did you know? The power of the LORD’s appearance is shown by the mountains melting and the valleys splitting open, like wax before the fire and water poured down a slope.

Did you know? Micah explains that the destruction results from Jacob’s transgression and the sins of the house of Israel, identifying Samaria as the center of Israel’s transgression and Jerusalem as the center of Judah’s high places.

Did you know? According to the prophecy, Samaria will become a ruin in the open country and a place for planting vineyards; its stones will be poured into the valley, and its foundations will be exposed.

Did you know? Samaria’s destruction includes the smashing of its idols, the burning of its images, and the demolition of its carved figures; the prophet also says that the wealth it accumulated will be taken away and returned to its source.
Did you know? Micah describes personal and public mourning over Samaria’s destruction: he will mourn, wail, go barefoot and naked, and grieve like the jackals and the ostriches.
Did you know? The blow does not stop at Samaria: according to the prophecy, it reaches Judah and even the gate of Jerusalem.

Did you know? In the final verses, Micah describes the disaster spreading through the towns of Judah in a series of calls to mourn, suffer disgrace, flee, and go into exile; finally, he calls on Daughter Zion to mourn for her beloved children who have gone into exile.
